title: Controversiae
author: Seneca the Elder
source: Translated by Claude from phi1014.phi001.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: CESTIVS dixit: uocaui filium; risit adulter tamquam qui diceret: meus est. VIBIVS RVFVS dixit: adulter meus exiit commodo suo. HYBREAS hunc sensum optime dixit DIONYSIVS, filius eius Dionysii qui Ciceronis filium docuit, elegans magis declamator quam uehemens, hunc sensum et uehementer dixit et eleganter VIBIVS RVFVS dixit:
passages.english: CESTIUS said: "I called my son; the adulterer laughed, as if to say: 'He is mine.'" VIBIUS RUFUS said: "My adulterer left at his own convenience." HYBREAS [...] This idea was expressed best by DIONYSIUS, son of the Dionysius who taught Cicero's son, a declaimer more elegant than forceful; VIBIUS RUFUS expressed this idea both forcefully and elegantly:
passages.notes: The text appears disordered or lacunose: 'HYBREAS' stands without a saying, and the sentence about Dionysius seems conflated with the following attribution to Vibius Rufus. The passage ends with a colon, so the quoted saying falls outside it.

passages.original: sed apparuit illas epistolas irascentis esse, non promittentis. In ultimo descripsit, quam miser futurus esset alimenta accipiens ab illis manibus, quas paulo ante spectauerit fratrem occidentes, et adiecit, quod aiebat praeceptore suo dicente summa cum admiratione exceptum, illud Homeri Priamo aptum: kai\ ku/se xei=ras deina/s, a)ndrofo/nous, ai(/ oi( pole/as kta/non ui(=as. SILO POMPEIVS et ipse iram fassus est.
passages.english: But it became clear that those letters were those of an angry man, not of one making a promise. At the end he described how wretched he would be, receiving his food from those hands which a little before he had watched killing his brother, and he added, a line which he said had been received with the greatest admiration when his teacher spoke it, that verse of Homer suited to Priam: "and he kissed the terrible, man-slaying hands, which had killed his many sons." SILO POMPEIUS too admitted anger.
passages.notes: Homer, Iliad 24.479; the Greek is given in Beta Code transliteration in the source.

passages.original: oratio eius iam tum nihil aliud poterat uideri quam solutum carmen. Adeo autem studiose Latronem audiit, ut multas illius sententias in uersus suos transtulerit. In armorum iudicio dixerat Latro : mittamus arma in hostis et petamus. Naso dixit: Arma uiri fortis medios mittantur in hostis; Inde iubete peti. et alium ex illa suasoria sensum aeque a Latrone mutuatus est. memini Latronem in praefatione quadam dicere, quod scolastici quasi carmen didicerant: non uides ut immota fax torpeat, ut exagitata reddat ignes?
passages.english: Even then his speech could seem nothing other than poetry set free from metre. He listened to Latro so eagerly that he transferred many of his epigrams into his own verses. In the 'Judgement of the Arms' Latro had said: "Let us throw the arms among the enemy and go to fetch them." Naso said: "Let the brave man's arms be thrown into the midst of the enemy; order them to be fetched from there." And he borrowed another idea from that suasoria, equally, from Latro. I remember Latro saying in a certain preface, a passage which the students had learned by heart like a poem: "Do you not see how a torch left unmoved grows dull, and how when shaken it gives back its fire?"
passages.notes: Naso is Ovid; the 'Judgement of the Arms' is the contest of Ajax and Ulysses (cf. Metamorphoses 13).

passages.original: imperator te tuus credidit posse parricidium facere. Abscidit caput, amputauit manum, effecit ut minimum in illo esset crimen quod Ciceronem occidit. Facinus indignum! felicissime licet cedat actio, id solum proficiemus, ut qui Ciceronem occidit tantum erubescat.
passages.english: Your commander believed you could commit parricide. He cut off the head, he cut off the hand; he brought it about that the least of the charges against him was that he killed Cicero. An outrageous crime! However successfully the prosecution may turn out, we shall achieve only this: that the man who killed Cicero merely blushes.

passages.original: a me defenditur Cicero, cum Popillium Cicero defenderit. MENTONIS. Non magis quisquam alius occidere Ciceronem potuit praeter Popillium, quam nemo Popillium praeter Ciceronem defendere. parricidam quem uiuos negarat Cicero occisus ostendit. Fortunam Ciceronis! Antonius illum proscripsit qui accusatus est, Popillius occidit qui defensus est. Si damnatus esses, carnifex te culleo tum insuisset. Video quid respondeat: non credet Antonius occisum Ciceronem a Popillio, nisi ei signum attulerit.
passages.english: Cicero is defended by me, though Cicero defended Popillius. [Saying] OF MENTO: No one other than Popillius could have killed Cicero, any more than anyone but Cicero could have defended Popillius. The man whom Cicero, while alive, had denied to be a parricide, Cicero once killed showed to be one. Cicero's fortune! Antony, whom he had accused, proscribed him; Popillius, whom he had defended, killed him. If you had been condemned, the executioner would then have sewn you into the sack. I see what he will reply: Antony will not believe that Cicero was killed by Popillius unless he brings him proof.
passages.notes: The culleus was the sack in which parricides were sewn and drowned. 'signum' could be 'token' or 'proof'.

passages.original: Securi erant amici Ciceronis postquam ad illum Popillius missus est. ARELLI FVSCI patris. Potuisti Ciceronem occidere? at quam nobis bene persuaserat Cicero parricidium te facere non posse! Occidisti tu Ciceronem loquentem: numquid, inquit, est aliquis ex tuis uerendus index? an nemo Ciceroni timendus est qui cum Popillio uenit? Q.
passages.english: Cicero's friends felt safe after Popillius was sent to him. [Saying] OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder: You were able to kill Cicero? And how well Cicero had persuaded us that you could not commit parricide! You killed Cicero as he was saying: "Surely there is no one among your men to be feared as an informer?" Or is no one who comes with Popillius to be feared by Cicero? Q.
passages.notes: The final 'Q.' is the praenomen of the next speaker, cut off.

passages.original: HATERI. Qui modo Italiae umeris relatus est nunc sic a Popillio refertur? proposito in rostris capite Ciceronis, quamuis omnia metu tenerentur, gemitus tamen populi liber fuit. IVLI BASSI. “Proscriptus, inquit, erat Cicero.” pater certe tuus proscriptus non fuit. Blandi. Di manes Popilli senis et inultae te patris, Cicero, persecuntur animae, ut quem negasti parricidam sentias. Capitonis. Deduxi ad uos reum omnium quos terra sustinet nocentissimum, ingratum, inpium, percussorem, bis parricidam;
passages.english: [Saying] OF HATERIUS: Is the man who not long ago was carried back on the shoulders of Italy now being carried back like this by Popillius? When Cicero's head was displayed on the rostra, although everything was gripped by fear, the groaning of the people was nonetheless free. [Saying] OF JULIUS BASSUS: "Cicero," he says, "was proscribed." Your father, at any rate, was not proscribed. [Saying] of Blandus: The shades of old Popillius and of your unavenged father pursue you, Cicero, so that you may feel [the hand of] the man you denied was a parricide. [Saying] of Capito: I have brought before you a defendant the guiltiest of all whom the earth sustains: ungrateful, impious, an assassin, twice a parricide;
passages.notes: The Blandus sentence seems corrupt ('te ... Cicero'); it may originally address Popillius, with Cicero's shade pursuing him. Translated as it stands.

passages.original: necesse certe non fuit manum caputque praecidere mortuo. Colorem pro Popillio Lateo simplicem habuit: necessitate coactum fecisse; et hoc loco illam sententiam dixit: miraris si eo tempore necesse fuit Popillio occidere quo Ciceroni mori? ALBVCIVS dixit in poenam Ciceronis electum amicissimum Ciceroni, quasi exprobraturus per hoc illi fortunam esset. molestius, inquit, feret se a Popillio occidi quam occidi. MARCELLVS AESERNINVS eundem colorem aliter induxit.
passages.english: Certainly it was not necessary to cut off the hand and head of a dead man. Latro had a simple 'colour' in Popillius' defence: that he acted under compulsion; and at this point he spoke this epigram: "Are you surprised if at that time it was necessary for Popillius to kill, when it was necessary for Cicero to die?" ALBUCIUS said that Cicero's closest friend had been chosen for Cicero's punishment, as if this was to reproach him with his fortune: "He will take it harder," he said, "to be killed by Popillius than to be killed." MARCELLUS AESERNINUS developed the same colour differently.
passages.notes: 'Lateo' is a scanning error for 'Latro'. 'Color' is the rhetorical term for the slant given to a case.

passages.original: offendebar, inquit, proscriptione et quaedam liberius loquebar. “Non miror; Ciceronis cliens es: tanto magis occide Ciceronem tuum.” Et dixit non suae infirmitatis sententiam: uterque, inquit, sed diuerso genere punitus est: Ciceronis proscriptio fuit occidi, mea occidere. MARVLLVS, praeceptor noster, sic narrauit: iussit, inquit, imperator, iussit uictor, iussit qui proscribebat: ego illi negare quicquam possem cui nihil poterat negare respublica?
passages.english: "I was offended," he said, "by the proscription and spoke somewhat too freely." "I am not surprised; you are Cicero's client: all the more reason, then, kill your Cicero." And he spoke an epigram not in keeping with his weakness: "Both of us," he said, "were punished, but in different ways: Cicero's proscription was to be killed, mine was to kill." MARULLUS, our teacher, narrated it thus: "The commander ordered it," he said, "the victor ordered it, the man conducting the proscription ordered it: could I refuse anything to him to whom the state could refuse nothing?"
passages.notes: The speaker of the opening is not named in this passage.

passages.original: “uocetur, inquit ille, Ciceronianus ille cliens, amicus; excogitaui quomodo Cicero sua periret manu.” CESTIVS hoc colore: durissima, inquit, mihi militia in Antonio castris fuit ob hoc ipsum quod Ciceronis eram cliens; difficillimae mihi expeditiones mandabantur. tunc quoque uocatus sum quasi ad poenam: “i, inquit, occide Ciceronem;
passages.english: "Let him be called," he [Antony] says, "that Ciceronian client, that friend; I have devised a way for Cicero to perish by his own hand." CESTIUS [used] this colour: "My military service in Antony's camp," he said, "was extremely harsh, for this very reason, that I was Cicero's client; the most difficult expeditions were assigned to me. Then too I was summoned as if to punishment: 'Go,' he said, 'kill Cicero;

passages.original: Latro ait: praecluserat fores; nemo ad proscriptum recipiebatur; Popillius ut uenit admissus est. CESTIVS dixit: ut renuntiatum est Ciceroni, ait: Popillio semper uaco. HISPANVS CORNELIVS fecit etiam querentem Ciceronem: Popilli, tam sero ? ALBVCIVS ait: quid est, Popilli? ecquid tuto lateo? numquid mutandus est locus ? Inepte † Sabidiebius PAVLVS qui induxit Ciceronem cum maxime pro Popillio orationem legentem. Et MVRREDIVS non est passus hanc controuersiam transire sine aliqua stuporis sui nota.
passages.english: Latro said: "He had shut his doors; no one was admitted to the proscribed man; Popillius, as soon as he came, was let in." Cestius said: "When it was announced to Cicero, he said: 'For Popillius I am always free.'" Cornelius Hispanus even had Cicero complaining: "Popillius, so late?" Albucius said: "What is it, Popillius? Am I hiding safely? Must I change my place?" Ineptly did Sabidienus(?) Paulus, who brought in Cicero reading, at that very moment, a speech in defence of Popillius. And Murredius did not let this controversia pass without some mark of his own stupidity.
passages.notes: The name rendered "Sabidienus Paulus" is obelized in the edition (†Sabidiebius); the true reading is uncertain.

passages.original: Pompei SILONIS. “Mihi, inquit, paraui.” et hoc est patri parare. Absolutus mori uolt, reus uiuit. MVSAE. “Habuit malum medicamentum Mithridates.” quis enim alius debebat habere quam parricida? “habuit, inquit, Demosthenes uenenum et bibit.” idem ego tibi pater quod Demostheni Philippus? Porci Latronis.
passages.english: Of Pompeius Silo: "'I prepared it for myself,' he says." And that is preparing it for his father. Acquitted, he wants to die; on trial, he lives. Of Musa: "'Mithridates had poison.'" Who else ought to have had it but a parricide? "'Demosthenes,' he says, 'had poison and drank it.'" Am I the same to you, as a father, as Philip was to Demosthenes? Of Porcius Latro.
passages.notes: The final heading "Of Porcius Latro" introduces a quotation that is not included in the passage.

passages.original: deinde auctorem huius uiti quod ex captione unius uerbi plura significantis nascitur aiebat POMPONIVM Atellanarum scriptorem fuisse, a quo primum ad LABERIVM transisse hoc studium imitandi, deinde inde ad Ciceronem qui illud ad uirtutem transtulissent. Nam ut transeam innumerabilia quae Cicero in orationibus aut in sermone dixit ex ea nota, ut non referam a Laberio dicta, cum mimi eius quidquid modo tolerabile habent tale habeant, id quod Cicero in Laberium diuus Iulius ludis suis mimum produxit, deinde equestri illum ordini reddidit;
passages.english: Then he said that the originator of this fault, which arises from catching at a single word with several meanings, was Pomponius, the writer of Atellan farces; from him this zeal for imitation passed first to Laberius, and then from there to Cicero, who turned it into a virtue. For, to pass over the countless things that Cicero said of this stamp in his speeches or in conversation, and not to repeat sayings of Laberius, since whatever is even tolerable in his mimes is of this kind, [I will cite] what Cicero [said] against Laberius. The deified Julius brought him on as a mime-actor at his games, and then restored him to the equestrian order;
passages.notes: The sentence "id quod Cicero in Laberium" appears to lack a verb, and the text may be defective; the sense is completed in brackets.

passages.original: Idem postea cum uideret a clientibus Catonis, rei sui, Pollionem Asinium circumuentum in foro caedi, inponi se supra cippum iussit — erat enim paruolus statura, propter quod etiam Catullus in hendecasyllabis uocat illum “salaputtium disertum” — et iurauit, si quam iniuriam Cato Pollioni Asinio accusatori suo fecisset, se in eum iuraturum calumniam; nec umquam postea Pollio a Catone aduocatisque eius aut re aut uerbo uiolatus est Solebat praeterea excedere subsellia sua et inpetu latus usque in aduersariorum partem transcurrere.
passages.english: The same man later, when he saw Asinius Pollio surrounded and being beaten in the forum by the clients of Cato, whom he was prosecuting, had himself set up on a pillar (for he was very small in stature, which is why Catullus too in his hendecasyllables calls him "an eloquent little mannikin"), and swore that if Cato did any injury to Asinius Pollio, his accuser, he himself would take the oath of malicious prosecution against him; and never afterwards was Pollio harmed by Cato and his advocates either in deed or in word. He used, moreover, to leave his own benches and, carried away by his impetus, run right across into his opponents' side.
passages.notes: "The same man" is Calvus (Licinius Calvus), from the surrounding context; "salaputtium" is a rare word of uncertain sense, perhaps "little man".

passages.original: A parte patris magis defensione opus esse dicebat Latro quam colore. VARIVS GEMINVS factum ipsum defendit: magnos uiros fecisse, ut libertinas uxores ducerent. M. Cato, inquit, coloni sui filiam duxit uxorem. “sed ingenuam.” respondeo: sed Cato: plus interest inter me et Catonem quam inter libertum et colonum. Quam multa commoda haberet subiectus et obsequens maritus. non petulantiam timebit, non uerborum contumeliam, non paelicem, non repudium.
passages.english: On the father's side, Latro said, there was more need of a defence than of a colour. Varius Geminus defended the deed itself: great men had married freedwomen. "Marcus Cato," he said, "married the daughter of his tenant farmer." "But she was freeborn." I reply: "But [he was] Cato: there is more difference between me and Cato than between a freedman and a tenant farmer." [He described] how many advantages a submissive and compliant husband would have: he will not fear insolence, nor abusive words, nor a mistress, nor divorce.
passages.notes: "Colour" (color) is the rhetorical term for the slant or explanation given to the facts of a case.

passages.original: Deinde factum liberti laudauit. ALBVCIVS et philosophatus est; dixit neminem natum liberum esse, neminem seruum; haec postea nomina singulis inposuisse fortunam. Denique, inquit, scis et nos nuper seruos fuisse. Retulit Seruium regem. SILO POMPEIVS hoc colore usus dixit: exhaustum tyrannidis iniuriis patrimonium; non habuisse se dotem quam daret. ARGENTARIVS uoluit uideri, puella uolente se fecisse. uisa est, inquit, indulgere illi;
passages.english: Then he praised the freedman's deed. ALBUCIUS even philosophised: he said that no one was born free, no one a slave; it was fortune that afterwards imposed these names on individuals. "Finally," he said, "you know that we too were slaves not long ago." He cited King Servius. SILO POMPEIUS used this colour and said: his patrimony had been exhausted by the injuries of the tyranny; he had not had a dowry to give. ARGENTARIUS wanted it to appear that he had acted with the girl's consent. "She seemed," he said, "to be fond of him;
passages.notes: "Colour" (color) is the technical rhetorical term for the slant or justification a declaimer gives to a character's conduct. "We too were slaves not long ago" presumably refers to the Romans' recent subjection (e.g. under the civil wars or the tyranny in the theme); the sense is not certain from the passage alone. The final clause runs on into the following context ("she certainly ought to have").

passages.original: Memini deinde Fuscum, cum haec Adaei sententia obiceretur, non infitiari transtulisse se eam in latinum, et aiebat non commendationis id se aut furti, sed exercitationis causa facere. Do, inquit, operam, ut cum optimis sententiis certem, nec illas corrumpere conor sed uincere. Tunc deinde retulit aliquam Thucydidis sententiam: deinai\ ga\r ai( eu)praci/ai sugkru/yai kai\ suskia/sai ta\ e(ka/stwn a(marth/mata, deinde Sallustianam: res secundae mire sunt uitiis optentui. cum sit praecipua in dide uirtus breuitas, hac eum Sallustius uicit et in suis illum castris cecidit;
passages.english: I remember, then, that Fuscus, when this epigram of Adaeus was thrown at him, did not deny that he had translated it into Latin, and he said that he did this not for credit or as theft but for practice. "I make it my effort," he said, "to compete with the best epigrams, and I do not try to spoil them but to surpass them." Then he cited a sentence of Thucydides: "For successes are terribly good at concealing and overshadowing each man's faults," and then Sallust's: "Prosperity is a wonderful screen for vices." Although brevity is the chief virtue in him [Thucydides], in this Sallust beat him and slew him in his own camp;
passages.notes: "in dide" is a scanning error, read as "in illo" or "in Thucydide".

passages.original: T. autem Liuius tam iniquus Sallustio fuit, ut hanc ipsam sententiam et tamquam translatam et tamquam corruptam dum transfertur obiceret Sallustio. nec hoc amore Thucydidis facit, ut illum praeferat, sed laudat quem non timet et facilius putat posse a se Sallustium uinci, si ante a Thucydide uincatur. CESTIVS colorem pro Callia hunc habuit: obiecit ultro Cimoni quod passus esset uxorem suam adulteram fieri, quod non custodisset, quod expectasset dum superueniret pater, ut spectator calamitatis suae fieret.
passages.english: But Titus Livy was so unfair to Sallust that he charged Sallust with this very epigram, both as translated and as spoiled in the translating. And he does this not out of love for Thucydides, to rank him higher, but he praises the one he does not fear, and thinks Sallust can more easily be beaten by himself if he is first beaten by Thucydides. Cestius took this colour on behalf of Callias: he went on the attack against Cimon for having allowed his wife to become an adulteress, for not having guarded her, for having waited until her father came upon them, so that he might become a spectator of his own disaster.

passages.original: P. VINICIVS summus amator Ouidi hunc aiebat sensum disertissime apud Nasonem Ouidium esse positum, quem ad fingendas similes sententias aiebat memoria tenendum. occiso Achille hoc epiphonema poni: quod Priamus gaudere senex post Hectora posset, hoc fuit. CASSIVS SEVERVS dixerat: ostende nobis captiuos tuos. IVLIVS BASSVS dixerat: ostende mercedarios tuos. LABIENVS commodius uidebatur dixisse: ostende nobis alumnos tuos. P. Asprenas dixit cum induxisset stipem porrigentem mendico: “o infelicem patrem!” et hoc qui dicit ipse fortassis pater est.
passages.english: Publius Vinicius, a great admirer of Ovid, used to say that this thought had been expressed most eloquently by Ovidius Naso, and he said it should be kept in memory for composing similar epigrams. When Achilles had been killed, this closing exclamation was used: "That over which old Priam could rejoice, after Hector, was this." Cassius Severus had said: "Show us your captives." Julius Bassus had said: "Show us your hirelings." Labienus seemed to have put it more aptly: "Show us your foster-children." Publius Asprenas, after bringing on [a figure] offering a coin to a beggar, said: "O unhappy father!" And the man who says this is perhaps himself a father.
passages.notes: The quoted Ovidian line is incomplete in this form; the first sentence's referent ("this thought") lies outside the passage. The Cassius Severus–Asprenas sayings appear to belong to a different controversia (on mutilated beggar children), and the text may be disordered here.
